transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in today?

Well, doc, the thing is... the reason they told me I had to come sit down with you is because my talking gets all mixed up. That's what they say, anyway. I'll be trying to explain something, just trying to have a regular conversation, but there's so much detail to it, you know? 

Like, I'll be at work—I clean the municipal building on the night shift—and I try to explain about the keys. The heavy brass ones on my ring, how they jingle and the specific weight of them in my pocket when I'm walking down the linoleum halls. But you can't really understand the keys unless I explain about the jail, because the locks on the third floor sound exactly like the holding cells down at the precinct, that loud metal clack echoing around. So I start talking about the jail, and the cold concrete floors there, which naturally brings me to the prayer rug. I was trying to tell my supervisor about the prayer rug, the one with the thick red fringe on the ends, because you need something soft on a floor like that, you have to have a barrier. And the pattern on that rug, it's got these geometric squares, so then I'm trying to explain about the chess pieces. The knights and the bishops, how they move across the squares, jumping over things, defending the king. 

It all connects, it makes perfect sense, but when I get to the chess pieces, people just put their hands up. They look at me like I'm speaking a different language. They tell me they cannot follow what I am saying. They say I'm jumping all over the place and my words are just a big tangled mess, going from keys to jails to rugs. I'm just trying to explain the whole picture so they get it, but they say they just can't follow me at all. So I guess that's what brings me in.
Do you ever strongly believe that other people are trying to harm you, watch you, or talk about you, even when there isn’t clear proof?

Well, doc, that's... that's a big question. It's a heavy question. And the thing is, I know how it sounds. I really do. But you have to understand what it's like when you're there, in the building, at night. The municipal building is old, you know, built back in the fifties, with these long, long hallways and those fluorescent lights that hum. They have this specific hum, like a low vibration that gets right into your teeth. 

And lately... well, not just lately, for a while now, I've been noticing things. Little things that add up. Like the way the lights flicker. Not just a normal flicker, but a pattern. It's like they're signaling. And the people who work late, the ones in the offices on the second floor, they give me these looks. Just these quick little side-eyes when I'm emptying the trash. It's like they know something. Like they've marked me. 

I tried to tell my supervisor, Mr. Henderson. I told him, "Mr. Henderson, they're watching me. They're using the lights and those little looks to warn each other." I explained the whole thing to him, the patterns, the way the hum of the lights changes when certain people walk by. He didn't believe me, of course. He took me down to the security room, showed me the camera feeds. He pointed at the screens and said, "Look, there's nothing there. It's just a building." 

And I looked at the screens, I really did. I saw the empty hallways. But seeing the screens didn't change how it felt in my gut. Even when he showed me there was nothing on the camera, I still felt it. I still felt absolutely sure that the building people had marked me. That they were using those hallway lights and those tiny little looks to communicate about me, warning each other. It's like the proof on the screen just didn't matter, because I knew what I felt, I knew what I was experiencing in those long, humming hallways. So, yes, I guess I do believe they're watching me, even when Mr. Henderson says there's no proof.
Do you think these people might actually be watching you, or do you know for sure they are?

Well, see, doc... that's the thing. Mr. Henderson, my supervisor, he tried to tell me I was just imagining things. He really did. He took me right down to the security room in the basement—it's this cramped little room, always smells like old coffee and floor wax down there—and he pointed right at the monitors. He said, "Look at the cameras, look at the screens, there's nobody there, there's nobody doing anything." And I looked. I stood there and I looked at those little black-and-white screens showing the empty hallways and the stairwells. 

But... and this is what I'm trying to explain, this is the crux of it... even when he showed me that nothing was on the camera, it didn't change a single thing for me. Not one bit. I still felt it in my bones. I still felt absolutely, one hundred percent sure that the building people had marked me. I know they are. I know for sure they are using those hallway lights, the way they flicker in that specific rhythm, and those little side-long looks they give each other when they think I'm just emptying the recycling bins... they're using all of that to warn each other about me. 

So, it's not a "might be" kind of thing, doc. It's not a guess. Mr. Henderson can point at his little screens all night long, but a camera doesn't catch everything. A camera doesn't catch the feeling in the air, or the meaning behind a look, or the exact pattern of a fluorescent bulb humming right before someone walks out of their office. I know what's happening. I know they've marked me. I know it for a fact, no matter what anyone else tries to show me.
Do you often avoid social situations because you feel very anxious about being judged, criticized, or embarrassed by other people?

Well, doc, no, it's not... it's not like that. I don't get anxious about people judging me or anything like that. It's not about being embarrassed. I don't care if they judge my sweeping technique or how I empty the bins, you know? I've been doing this kind of work for a long time, since I left school back in the tenth grade, and I know how to handle a mop and a bucket. 

The thing is, I don't avoid people because I'm worried they'll criticize me. I avoid them because of the other stuff. The stuff I was just telling you about. The marking. The way they communicate with the lights and those looks. It's not a fear of being embarrassed, it's... it's a matter of safety, of knowing who is involved in this whole thing. 

Like, take the breakroom on the second floor. I used to go in there to eat my sandwich around 2:00 AM. It's got this old vending machine that hums almost as loud as the lights, and these plastic chairs that scrape on the linoleum. But I stopped going in there. Not because I was worried they'd judge my ham and cheese sandwich, but because the people who work late, the ones from the accounting department, they'd come in and just... stand there. They'd stand by the coffee maker and they wouldn't even make coffee. They'd just wait until I looked up, and then they'd do that little side-eye thing to each other. 

So I don't avoid social situations because of some kind of social anxiety or whatever you call it. I just stay away from them because I know what they're doing. I know they're part of it. I'd rather just stay out of their way, stick to my floors, keep my head down, and watch the patterns. But it's definitely not because I'm scared they're going to embarrass me or something. It's much, much bigger than that.
Have you had these kinds of social-communication difficulties since childhood?

Childhood? No, doc, you're... I think you're looking in the wrong place with that one. You're barking up the wrong tree entirely. When I was a kid, growing up, I was just like anybody else. I had buddies. Me and this kid Jimmy, we used to hang out all the time, talked about whatever kids talk about. I never had any trouble understanding what people meant or talking to them. Even when I got to high school, right up until I left in the tenth grade to start working, I was completely fine with people. I talked, they talked, we understood each other. There wasn't any... what did you call it? Social-communication difficulty. I didn't have any of that. 

You keep trying to make this about me having some kind of lifelong problem, like my brain doesn't know how to talk to people or something. But you're missing the point, doc. You're missing the whole reality of the situation. The point is what's happening right now. I didn't have people blinking fluorescent lights at me in a pattern when I was twelve years old, you know? Jimmy wasn't giving me side-eyes to warn the neighborhood kids about me. This is specific to the municipal building. It's specific to the people who work late on the second floor. 

It's not a communication difficulty on my end at all. In fact, it's the exact opposite! I understand perfectly well what they're communicating. That's the whole issue here. I see the patterns in the lights, I see the exact way they look at each other when I walk by with the mop bucket. If I had a communication problem, I wouldn't be able to read their signals so clearly, would I? I'd just be oblivious. But I'm not oblivious. I see exactly what they're doing, and I've been trying to tell you and Mr. Henderson both, it's not a problem with how I talk to people. It's what they are doing to me.
How certain are you that the people at the building are watching or targeting you?

Certain? Doc, I feel like we're going in circles here, like you're just not hearing what I've been saying this whole time. I'm a hundred percent certain. A thousand percent. Like I told you just a few minutes ago about Mr. Henderson and that cramped little security room down in the basement... he really thought he was doing me a favor, you know? He thought he could just point at those fuzzy little black-and-white monitors showing the empty third-floor corridor—the one where the floor wax is always peeling up near the baseboards—and that would just magically make me change my mind. He kept tapping the glass on the screen, saying, "See? Nobody's there." 

But looking at an empty screen doesn't erase what I know in my gut. I told him then, and I'm telling you now, seeing nothing on a camera didn't change a single thing for me. Because a camera is just... it's just a machine, doc. It's stupid. It doesn't pick up the real stuff. It doesn't pick up the fact that I am absolutely, undeniably sure that the people in that building have marked me. 

You ask how certain I am? I'm so certain because I see it happening right in front of my face every single shift. The cameras don't record the way those fluorescent tubes above the water cooler flicker—bzz-bzz, pause, bzz—in that exact same rhythm right when the guys from the tax office walk past my cart. A camera lens can't capture the heavy, thick feeling in the air, or those little sideways glances they shoot each other right over my head. They look at each other like I'm just part of the furniture, just the old guy with the mop who doesn't know any better. But they're using those looks, and they're using those lights, to warn each other that I'm there. 

So, yeah, I'm certain. Asking me if I'm certain is like asking me if I know my own name or if I know how to mix the industrial floor cleaner. It's a fact of my life now. Henderson can stare at his monitors until his eyes cross, but I'm the one out there in the hallways, and I know exactly what they're doing to me.
